lead: Test automation means using software to run pre-written checks without a person clicking each step. It exists because regression suites grow while release cycles shrink. A manual suite that takes six person-hours per run becomes a bottleneck when the team releases every week. Automation is used for stable checks that repeat: smoke tests, regression tests, API checks, load tests and data-heavy validation. The decision is economic, not emotional: automate the tests that are run often and change rarely, after comparing build cost, run cost and maintenance against manual effort.
prereq: You need: Unit 4 test types and test case design, and 5.1, where the test plan fixes the automation scope.

blocks.text: Automation is code that runs a check without a person. It pays back when the same check runs many times. The test plan from 5.1 should list candidates before any tool is chosen. Automate checks that are stable, repeatable, high-volume, data-driven and part of regression or smoke suites. API checks and performance tests are strong candidates because they are fast and call little user interface.

Do not automate a feature whose rules change daily. Do not automate exploratory testing: its value is the human judgement that chooses the next step. Usability testing needs a person to judge confusion. A one-off migration check will not repay its build cost.

items: Good candidates: regression suite, smoke suite, API contract checks, load tests, data-driven validation, build verification.
Poor candidates: new user interface, exploratory sessions, usability review, one-off checks.

blocks.where: R is break-even regression runs; B is build effort in person-hours; M is manual effort per run in person-hours; A is automated maintenance effort per run in person-hours. Automate when planned runs exceed R.

sections.h3: Design styles and the test pyramid

blocks.text: A design style is the shape of the test code. Linear scripts record steps in order; they are quick to start and costly to maintain. Modular scripts call reusable functions. Data-driven tests keep data in tables, and one script reads many rows. Keyword-driven tests give each action a word, so a non-programmer can write cases. Hybrid designs mix these. The page object model gives each web page a class; tests call page methods, not raw selectors. Behaviour-driven tests write steps in plain language and bind them to code.

The test pyramid sets the mix. Put many tests at unit level, fewer at API level, and few at UI level. Unit tests are fast and stable. API tests are slower but still robust. UI tests are slow, need a browser, and break when layout changes. A UI-heavy suite gives late, flaky feedback.

items: Unit layer: JUnit, TestNG or PyTest, milliseconds per test.
API layer: Postman collections, seconds per test.
UI layer: Selenium or Playwright for web; Appium for mobile, tens of seconds per test.
Behaviour layer: Cucumber scenarios for business-readable checks.

sections.h3: Tools, return on investment and maintenance

blocks.text: Choose a tool by criteria, not by fashion. Check language and platform support, licence cost, CI integration, reporting, community size and team skill. A tool the team cannot debug is a liability.

blocks.text: Return on investment has three parts. Build cost is the one-time effort to write the suite. Run cost is machine time and people time to execute it. Maintenance cost is the ongoing effort after a product change. Maintenance is the part teams underestimate: selectors break, test data ages, and waits fail. A suite that is not maintained becomes a false alarm generator.

Keep test code in version control with the product code. Review it like product code: names, structure, data handling and assertions. Run it in the pipeline from 5.6 and 5.7. A test that only runs on one engineer's laptop is not automation; it is a demo.

figure.caption: Manual effort rises by 6 person-hours per run; automation starts at 60 and rises by 2. The lines cross at 15 runs, the break-even point.

spec.aria: Two straight lines on a plot: manual effort 6x and automated effort 60+2x, crossing at 15 runs and 90 person-hours.

examples.question: A 120-case regression suite is run 12 times a year. Manual cost is 6 person-hours per run. Automation needs 60 person-hours to build, then 2 person-hours per run for maintenance. Should the team automate? Find year-1 costs, break-even runs, and the three-year saving.
steps: Manual cost per run is 6 person-hours. Over 12 runs: 6 × 12 = 72 person-hours.
Build cost is 60 person-hours. Maintenance is 2 person-hours per run. Year 1 automated cost: 60 + 2 × 12 = 84 person-hours.
Year 1 difference: 84 − 72 = 12 person-hours more than manual, so automation loses in year 1.
Break-even runs: R = 60 ÷ (6 − 2) = 15 runs. At 12 runs a year, time = 15 ÷ 12 = 1.25 years = 15 months.
Saving: 216 − 132 = 84 person-hours. Decision: automate, because the suite will also grow and the product will be maintained for years.
examples.answer: Automate: the suite breaks even at 15 runs, about 15 months, and saves 84 person-hours over 3 years.
examples.check:
manual_per_run = 6
runs_per_year = 12
build = 60
maintenance = 2

manual_year = manual_per_run * runs_per_year
auto_year = build + maintenance * runs_per_year
year1_diff = auto_year - manual_year
break_even_runs = build // (manual_per_run - maintenance)
break_even_years = break_even_runs / runs_per_year
manual_3 = manual_per_run * 3 * runs_per_year
auto_3 = build + maintenance * 3 * runs_per_year
saving = manual_3 - auto_3

print(manual_year)
print(auto_year)
print(year1_diff)
print(break_even_runs)
print(break_even_years)
print(manual_3)
print(auto_3)
print(saving)

traps: Automation does not replace manual testing; it repeats known checks. It finds regression, not new defects.
Forgetting maintenance cost: a suite with high maintenance may never break even.
Automating unstable features: the script churns with the feature and becomes waste.
An inverted pyramid: many slow UI tests and few unit tests, giving slow and flaky feedback.
Treating record-and-playback as design: it creates linear scripts that break on the first change.

quiz.q: Define test automation and state one test type it suits.
quiz.a: Test automation runs pre-written checks by software, without a person clicking each step. It suits regression or smoke tests.

quiz.q: Why is a rapidly changing feature a poor automation candidate?
quiz.a: Its expected behaviour changes before the script repays build cost. Scripts need frequent rework, so maintenance can exceed manual effort.

quiz.q: A suite is run 20 times a year. Manual cost is 5 person-hours per run. Build cost is 80 person-hours; maintenance is 3 person-hours per run. Find break-even runs, year-1 manual cost, year-1 automated cost, and the year-1 difference.
quiz.a: Break-even runs = 80 ÷ (5 − 3) = 40 runs. Year-1 manual = 5 × 20 = 100 person-hours. Year-1 automated = 80 + 3 × 20 = 140 person-hours. Difference = 140 − 100 = 40 person-hours more, so automation loses in year 1.

quiz.q: A team has 300 UI tests taking 6 hours in CI, while unit tests take 2 minutes. State the pyramid problem and one redesign.
quiz.a: It is an inverted pyramid: too many slow UI tests and too few fast unit tests. Redesign by moving checks to unit and API layers and keeping a few critical UI journeys.
Linear scripts, modular scripts, data-driven tests and keyword-driven tests. Hybrid designs, page object model and behaviour-driven tests are further styles.

quiz.q: A team knows Java, needs web and mobile UI tests, and has a small budget. Name two tool selection criteria and one tool for each UI layer.
quiz.a: Criteria: language support for Java and licence cost or total cost. Web UI: Selenium or Playwright. Mobile UI: Appium.

quiz.q: Why is ignoring maintenance the second error after believing automation replaces manual testing?
quiz.a: Maintenance raises A in R = B ÷ (M − A). If A approaches M, break-even never arrives. The suite also becomes flaky, so the team stops trusting it.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry now leans on Playwright and Cypress for web, contract tests such as Pact for services, and flaky-test dashboards in CI. AI-assisted locators and test generation are emerging, but the pyramid and ROI reasoning still decide what to keep.
